# Philosophy & Ethics — BATCH 1: Dense Observations (2015-03-14 to 2017-01-13)

---

## RECURRING ARGUMENTS FF MAKES

### Purpose Over Profit
FF consistently argues that great businesses are animated by purpose, not profit maximization. Tim Cook's words are quoted approvingly: "Making money might be a by-product, but it's not our North Star." — SOURCE: "Why chasing profit may be self defeating" by Founding Fuel (2015-04-06)

This is framed as the "Inside-Outside Way of Thinking" — the inner circle is *why* the company exists, the outer is *what* it does. — SOURCE: "Why chasing profit may be self defeating" by Founding Fuel (2015-04-06)

Raj Sisodia's Conscious Capitalism movement is cited: "just as a few human beings set great purposes for themselves and eventually achieve greatness, the best companies in the world have great purposes." — SOURCE: "The search for higher purpose" by Indrajit Gupta (2015-03-16)

### Integrity as Strategic Capital, Not Just Morality
Integrity is framed economically — "reputation, built on a sustained view of governance, has its own return on investment. Even the retail investor has eyes and ears." — SOURCE: "Integrity versus high performance" by Founding Fuel (2015-11-04)

"People learn what is, and what is not, the accepted organisation behaviour, not through 'company policy' but, company action. Only action creates social memory." — SOURCE: "Integrity versus high performance" by Founding Fuel (2015-11-04)

### Entrepreneurship Is Not for Everyone
FF explicitly and repeatedly pushes back against the "cult of entrepreneurship." "Not everyone should be an entrepreneur... hoping that many more people in India should be entrepreneurs is NOT the same as believing that everyone should be an entrepreneur." — SOURCE: "Why not to be an entrepreneur" by Founding Fuel (2015-03-30)

FF also distinguishes between *entrepreneurial* (a temperament, nearly universally prescribable) and *entrepreneur* (starting a business, not for everyone). — SOURCE: "Why not to be an entrepreneur" by Founding Fuel (2015-03-30)

### The Danger of Envy and False Comparison
Staying motivated when rivals raise more money is treated as a philosophical/ethical problem: "For every entrepreneur, there are many distractions, of which, jealousy is one." — SOURCE: "Staying motivated when rivals raise a lot more money" by Founding Fuel (2015-08-31)

The Mindtree origin story is used as evidence: Scient, Viant, Razorfish raised 5-10x more but ended in "graveyards." Mindtree raised only $23.5M before IPO in 2007. — SOURCE: "Staying motivated when rivals raise a lot more money" by Founding Fuel (2015-08-31)

### Complexity and Size Are Not Virtues
"Everything has an appropriate size." FF regularly invokes JBS Haldane's Square-Cube law to argue against the "altar of bigger." Having 5 million customers is not always preferable to 50,000. — SOURCE: "The altar of bigger" by Founding Fuel (2015-06-08)

"We seldom display this understanding. In our default mental position, a $10 million company is the same as another with $1 million in sales, only bigger and better." — SOURCE: "The altar of bigger" by Founding Fuel (2015-06-08)

### Leaders Need Warmth, Not Just Competence
High competence + low warmth = the "envy" quadrant. Leaders need both. Source is Amy Cuddy, Susan Fiske, and Peter Glick (HBR July-August 2014). The message: move from "envy" to "admired." — SOURCE: "How to be a High-Impact Leader" by Founding Fuel (2015-04-15)

### Technology Addiction as a Genuine Ethical/Wellbeing Crisis
FF treats internet addiction with the same seriousness as drug addiction — same dopamine loops, same withdrawal behavior, same brain centers. RescueTime data self-reported: 40% of laptop time on distracting tasks. FitBit data: 4:17 hours average sleep. — SOURCE: "Confessions of a recovering junkie" by Charles Assisi (2015-03-28)

### The Limits of "Doing Nothing"
FF is skeptical of the aspiration to retire early and "do nothing." Four fallacies identified: money unlocks life's prizes; free time enables self-actualization; humans are designed for simple lives; peaceful conflict-free lives are optimal. — SOURCE: "The Inglorious Goal of Doing Nothing" by Founding Fuel (2015-04-20)

"Complexity is not our enemy. The human neocortical brain is designed for more complexity than a dog." — SOURCE: "The Inglorious Goal of Doing Nothing" by Founding Fuel (2015-04-20)

### Deliberate Cheating Is Categorically Different From Negligence
VW's cheat software is carefully distinguished from Toyota's stuck accelerator or J&J's Tylenol poisoning. "While the other cases were the result of either an uncontrollable event... in the case of Volkswagen, it is deliberate cheating." — SOURCE: "Volkswagen: The Difficulty of Being Good and the Ease of Being a Cheat" by Baba Prasad (2015-10-09)

## FF'S INDIA-SPECIFIC ANGLE

### India's Literacy-Employment Mismatch
Kerala's chayakadas (tea stalls) become a lens on India's structural problem — a "hugely literate population that cannot find suitable jobs to match their skill sets." The ghost-writing PhD business is used to examine how commoditized, generic writing (indistinguishable from wire-service copy) is both a symptom and a product of this mismatch. — SOURCE: "Doctoral dissertations from a tea stall" by Charles Assisi (2015-05-24)

### India's Corruption Culture as Systemic, Not Aberrational
A VC's story of mobile gaming startup budgeting ₹5 crore for "under-the-table" payments to VAS teams at cellular operators — called "standard industry practice." This is presented as an ecosystem-level ethical failure, not individual corruption. "Greed happens at four levels" — politicians, corporates, middle class, individual. — SOURCE: "The End of Innocence" by Haresh Chawla (2015-10-27)

The Assocham/Grant Thornton data cited: 71% of companies surveyed expected corporate fraud cases to increase. — SOURCE: "The End of Innocence" by Haresh Chawla (2015-10-27)

### Indian Entrepreneurship Needs Its Own Mythology
Young Indian entrepreneurs reference Elon Musk, Bezos, Zuckerberg but not NR Narayana Murthy or Azim Premji, let alone 19th-century paragons like Laxmanrao Kirloskar or Jamsetji Tata. The Promethean (Western) model — endless expansion, exploitation of nature — is contrasted against an Indian model still being articulated. — SOURCE: "What is Indian about the Indian entrepreneur?" by Baba Prasad (2016-08-14)

India now has 19,000 tech-enabled startups, 48 million small businesses (more than twice the US count), and 8 unicorns (as of Dec 2015). — SOURCE: "What is Indian about the Indian entrepreneur?" by Baba Prasad (2016-08-14)

### India's Cancer Care Gap as Ethics Issue
India has ~1 million new cancer patients yearly; only 150,000 get treatment. 80% 5-year breast cancer survival in Finland, vs 12% overall in India. Framed as a systemic ethical failure of the innovation ecosystem to address actual human need. — SOURCE: "The state of cancer research and the future of innovation" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2016-03-08)

### Gujarat Riots as Business Ethics Watershed
The 2002 Gujarat riots as a moment when Indian business leaders had to decide whether to speak up — the AIMA meeting in Mumbai that produced the concept of the "ladder of business responsibility." — SOURCE: "Climbing the ladder of business responsibility" by Arun Maira (2015-11-11)

Royal Dutch Shell/Nigeria parallel drawn explicitly: silence as complicity. — SOURCE: "Climbing the ladder of business responsibility" by Arun Maira (2015-11-11)

### Indian Fake Followers Economy
₹400 for 1,000 "cheap" Twitter followers. ₹3,000 for manually created Indian handles. Sweatshops in Delhi and Bangladesh generating fake social media influence. Politicians and businessmen audited on Twitter Audit tool. — SOURCE: "How to buy friends and influence people" by Charles Assisi (2015-05-10)

### FreeCharge's Behavioral Insight Model
Kunal Shah's FreeCharge built on behavioral understanding ("brag-worthy" proposition that drove offline-to-online habit change without heavy marketing spend). Philosophy degree cited as more valuable than MBA for business. Apple Macbook with offer letter as an early trust/ethics litmus test for hiring. — SOURCE: "Kunal Shah: 'Understanding humans is core to great businesses'" by Founding Fuel (2017-01-13)

### Abdul Kalam as Ethical Leadership Model
Kalam's daily commitment to visit three schools per day during his presidency — "If ceremonial duties come in the way of that, I will make up for the deficit the next day" — held up as exemplary self-management in Drucker's sense. His self-aware acknowledgment that he gave "politically correct answers" at the Rashtrapati Bhavan session is treated as a model of intellectual honesty. — SOURCE: "Why Abdul Kalam continues to matter" by Charles Assisi (2016-01-12)

### Recurring Mental Models
- **2×2 Matrix (Love vs. Competence)** — For evaluating entrepreneurial fit: the "magic quadrant" of high love + high competence is "the Steve Jobs stuff." — SOURCE: "The love versus competence debate" by Founding Fuel (2015-03-17)
- **Hindu Trinity as Organizational Framework** — Brahma (founder/creator), Vishnu (professional CEO/sustainer), Shiva (creative destroyer). Used to argue for complementary competencies and self-knowledge. "Even Gods are not 'super-humans', they are not multi-skilled." — SOURCE: "Having that sense of wonder" by Founding Fuel (2015-03-30)
- **The Ladder of Business Responsibility** — Five rungs from investor accountability up through political citizenship. — SOURCE: "Climbing the ladder of business responsibility" by Arun Maira (2015-11-11)

- **The Innovator's DNA** (Christensen) — Five behaviors: associating, questioning, observing, networking, experimenting. — SOURCE: "Lessons from the road" by Charles Assisi (2016-07-11)

# Philosophy & Ethics — Batch 2 Raw Observations (2017-01-16 to 2017-11-26)

---

## RECURRING ARGUMENTS FF MAKES

**On media's democratic failure:**
FF argues media has abandoned its civic role by becoming purely commercial. "The media must not become a business like any other business" — the tension between giving audiences "what they want" versus what they need for democratic participation is framed as a civilizational problem. — SOURCE: "How the media has let down democracy" by Arun Maira (2017-01-16)

FF explicitly frames its own "less is more" editorial philosophy as a counter to media dumbing-down: "We've been feeding this self-fulfilling prophesy that readers don't have time for anything in-depth." — SOURCE: "Creating space for reflection" by Founding Fuel (2017-03-06)

**On polarisation as a designed phenomenon:**
FF repeatedly argues that binary, polarised discourse is not organic — it is *engineered*. "Because it is designed to be that way. There's a sucker born every minute." — SOURCE: "Two idiots and three pigs" by Charles Assisi (2017-05-05)

The same argument extends to Aadhaar debates, liberal-conservative splits, and tech discourse: "we live in polarised times." — SOURCE: "The Aadhaar debate: Is common ground possible?" by NS Ramnath (2017-06-17)

**On the necessity of reflection and slowness:**
FF persistently advocates for deliberate pauses against the "treadmill of activity." "It is only by slowing things down—and being more reflective—do we allow our best selves to emerge." — SOURCE: "Creating space for reflection" by Founding Fuel (2017-03-06)

Tony Schwartz's observation that "the opposite of action is inaction" has been wrongly "demonised" is cited as a diagnosis of contemporary leadership pathology. — SOURCE: "Creating space for reflection" by Founding Fuel (2017-03-06)

**On technology being neither utopian nor dystopian:**
FF consistently rejects binary positions on technology. The "sceptical optimist" frame is held up as the correct posture: "Approach it the way you would look at buying a house. Know what's good, know what's bad." — SOURCE: "The Sceptical Optimist" by NS Ramnath (2017-04-21)

The same frame is applied to Aadhaar: "What if we keep our own ideology and our views on others' intent aside, and look at the entire debate much like the way we would if we plan to buy a house or a car?" — SOURCE: "The Aadhaar debate: Is common ground possible?" by NS Ramnath (2017-06-17)

**On privacy as a civilisational challenge, not merely an Aadhaar issue:**
"Privacy is a much bigger issue. To see it only through the lens of Aadhaar — even though it has an urgency — is to miss the bigger picture." — SOURCE: "Yes, we need privacy protection. No, it's not just about Aadhaar" by NS Ramnath (2017-07-26)

**On data as the new oil — with an important corrective:**
"In much the same way that natural resources like minerals and oil were mined in earlier decades, everyone's data is being mined. It is now the most precious resource." But FF adds a critical twist: unlike oil, data is infinite. And the Middle East oil analogy warns that those sitting on the resource often don't know its value and concede control cheaply. — SOURCE: "A brief history of money, identity and Aadhaar" by Charles Assisi (2017-07-24)

**On constraints as creativity:**
FF returns repeatedly to the idea that constraints — financial, material, temporal — are generative rather than limiting. Jugaad, Eliyahu Goldratt's Theory of Constraints, Carlos Ghosn's "frugal engineering," and Hemingway's six-word story are all marshalled for this argument. — SOURCE: "Moderate constraints actually boost creativity" by Charles Assisi (2017-04-22)

**On purpose beyond money:**
"Business was no more about making money than being human is about making blood." Phil Knight's Nike story is used to argue that transformative enterprises are built on missions that transcend financial metrics. — SOURCE: "In pursuit of purpose" by Founding Fuel (2017-06-11)

This recurs in Arun Maira's meditation on Gandhi: "There is too much focus on achievement of ends (wealth, size, fame) that society measures and applauds. And too little attention to the means." — SOURCE: "Tune inwards, define your 'why'" by Founding Fuel (2017-06-25)

**On leadership and the danger of not letting go:**
Multiple articles circle the same pathology: leaders who cannot release their identity from institutions they built. Narayana Murthy is the case study: "Is there a creature who did not learn when it is time to let go?" — SOURCE: "What is the matter with men like NR Narayana Murthy?" by Charles Assisi (2017-07-18)

Yann Martel's distinction is invoked: "Fanatics do not have faith — they have belief. With faith you let go. You trust. Whereas with belief you cling." — SOURCE: "What is the matter with men like NR Narayana Murthy?" by Charles Assisi (2017-07-18)

**On AI augmenting rather than replacing humans:**
FF's consistent editorial line is cautious optimism about AI. Kasparov's *Deep Thinking* and Brad Nelson's robotics perspective both arrive at augmentation, not replacement. "I am not at all afraid that it is replacing people." — SOURCE: "Can artificial intelligence augment humankind?" by CKGSB Knowledge (2017-09-02)

**On listening as a leadership skill:**
Arun Maira's work provides FF with a recurring framework: listening to "people not like us" is both a leadership tool and a civilisational necessity. The Dalai Lama's formulation is quoted: "Listening is the first of the three wisdom tools in Buddhist tradition." — SOURCE: "The battle for our data" by Founding Fuel (2017-09-10)

## FF'S INDIA-SPECIFIC ANGLE

**Jugaad as philosophical system, not mere hack:**
FF elevates jugaad beyond the condescending "frugal innovation" label used in the West: "Jugaad is embedded in our psyche—by our very nature, we are built to make do with less." Chit funds and kirana stores are held up as sophisticated trust-based systems that Western management theory is only now theorising. — SOURCE: "Moderate constraints actually boost creativity" by Charles Assisi (2017-04-22)

**India transitioning from data-poor to data-rich — an unprecedented situation:**
"What we are witnessing now is an 'economically poor' nation migrating to being a 'data-rich' nation. This is unprecedented in history." FF argues existing legal frameworks (built for wealthy, data-rich societies) don't fit India's context. — SOURCE: "The future of privacy: A conversation with Rahul Matthan" by Founding Fuel (2017-09-17)

**India's governance failures in public health as a moral failure:**
The Gorakhpur encephalitis deaths are treated as evidence of a broken public health system and systemic apathy. "Those kids who have died... are perhaps better off dead. Because if they'd survived, life may have been crueller to them." — SOURCE: "A tryst with insanity, encephalitis and apathy" by Charles Assisi (2017-08-20)

The contrast with Sri Lanka and Nepal's success in eradicating Japanese Encephalitis is used to argue India's failure is political will, not capability. — SOURCE: "A tryst with insanity, encephalitis and apathy" by Charles Assisi (2017-08-20)

**India's "promoter culture" as a governance distortion:**
"Love thy promoters. Thou shall not question their divine right to run the board." Rama Bijapurkar argues Infosys is a rare exception to India's promoter-dominated corporate culture, making the Murthy battle uniquely instructive. SEBI only in 2015 "considered the possibility that a non-promoter-run company could exist." — SOURCE: "Why Narayana Murthy needs to relearn the rules of the Murthy Doctrine" by Rama Bijapurkar (2017-08-20)

**India's liberal vacuum:**
FF makes a pointed India-specific argument: "I am hard-pressed to think of contemporary Indian liberals." The so-called liberal camp is critiqued for dogmatism that mirrors the orthodoxy it claims to oppose. "When confronted with evidence from multiple fronts on the benefits of technology, the conversation degenerates." — SOURCE: "The myth that is the Indian liberal" by Charles Assisi (2017-06-03)

**Aadhaar as a uniquely Indian experiment in identity:**
FF frames Aadhaar not simply as a tech or governance project but as a philosophical reckoning: "To understand it, voices from disciplines as diverse as history, philosophy, politics, entrepreneurship and artificial intelligence must be accessed." — SOURCE: "The Aadhaar Effect" by Founding Fuel (2017-07-30)

**Inequality as India's most pressing ethical question:**
NS Ramnath's framing of what future generations will find abhorrent — "That so many of us live in luxury, while a large number of our fellow human beings go to bed hungry" — is explicitly connected to Indian capitalism. Yunus's social business model is positioned as more resonant in India than in the West. — SOURCE: "Muhammad Yunus and the two visions of Adam Smith" by NS Ramnath (2017-11-11)

**Airport boarding-pass scanning as privacy microcosm:**
A mundane Indian airport encounter becomes FF's vehicle for a systemic point: "Pretty much everybody can be compromised by either the state or any private entity." India's "tech capital" population meekly handing over biometric-linked data without awareness is treated as symptomatic. — SOURCE: "We're getting de-FANGed and Uber-ed" by Charles Assisi (2017-07-02)

---

## FRAMEWORKS, THINKERS, MENTAL MODELS

**Nicholas Agar's "Sceptical Optimism":** Applied throughout to technology debates, Aadhaar, AI. The house-purchase analogy ("know what's good, know what's bad") becomes FF's go-to heuristic for navigating tech polarisation. — SOURCE: "The Sceptical Optimist" by NS Ramnath (2017-04-21); "The Aadhaar debate: Is common ground possible?" by NS Ramnath (2017-06-17)

**Theory of Constraints (Eliyahu Goldratt):** Appears in multiple articles as the intellectual backbone of the constraints-as-creativity argument. Extended to personal productivity and leadership. — SOURCE: "Moderate constraints actually boost creativity" by Charles Assisi (2017-04-22); "The Tao of thinking" by Charles Assisi (2017-05-20)

**Will and Ariel Durant's *The Lessons of History*:** Used as a corrective to technological utopianism. "Everything repeats itself. Over. And over. Again." Applied specifically to AI hype. — SOURCE: "Life is unfair. Deal with it" by Charles Assisi (2017-07-10)

**Michael Sandel's framework on markets and moral limits:** Invoked via the Aspen seminar anecdote — the drug dealer analogy for media — to argue businesses cannot use "giving people what they want" as moral cover. — SOURCE: "How the media has let down democracy" by Arun Maira (2017-01-16)

**Nassim Nicholas Taleb's Anti-Fragility:** The concept of being anti-fragile — not merely resilient — is applied to individual psychology, leadership, and intellectual life. Leonardo da Vinci and Einstein are held up as examples. Taleb's graduation speech definition of success ("you look in the mirror every evening, and wonder if you disappoint the person you were at 18") becomes a moral touchstone. — SOURCE: "The absence of fragility" by Charles Assisi (2017-11-12)

**Nate Silver's signal/noise framework:** Used to argue that Twitter's 140-character limit structurally *forces* inaccuracy — you can only get to statement #4 of a 7-part increasingly nuanced proposition about efficient markets. — SOURCE: "Aadhaar, Twitter and strong opinions, loosely held" by NS Ramnath (2017-10-01)

**Kahneman/Tversky behavioural economics:** The Nobel laureate interview establishes that rationality is a fiction — "people sometimes make decisions that appear to be quite counter to their own interests" — as a foundation for FF's broader skepticism of market-based justifications. — SOURCE: "Less-than-rational actors" by CKGSB Knowledge (2017-09-28)

**Primed to Perform (Neel Doshi & Lindsay McGregor):** A chart on motivations for work is reproduced to contextualise how economic and emotional forces shape career choices. — SOURCE: "Why we do what we do, and where does money come into it" by Charles Assisi (2017-06-09)

**Roman Krznaric's *How to Find Fulfilling Work*:** The Jackson Pollock painting anecdote (prison cell viewed from inside vs. outside) becomes a framework for understanding generational differences in how freedom is experienced. — SOURCE: "Why we do what we do, and where does money come into it" by Charles Assisi (2017-06-09)

**Csikszentmihalyi on flow and creative deadening:** Resources can make people "too comfortable" — the doctoral thesis quote suggests abundance kills creativity. — SOURCE: "The Tao of thinking" by Charles Assisi (2017-05-20)

**Godwin's Law:** Cited to describe the velocity of online debate deterioration. "As if Godwin's Law is on steroids these days." — SOURCE: "The Aadhaar debate: Is common ground possible?" by NS Ramnath (2017-06-17)

**Buddha's Middle Path:** Applied to Aadhaar policy — not permissive (US approach) nor prohibitive (European approach) but precautionary. Jairam Ramesh's invocation of the middle path for GM food is cross-applied. — SOURCE: "Aadhaar and the Buddha's Middle Path" by Founding Fuel (2017-11-06)

**Rahul Matthan's rights-based model vs. consent model:** A specific legal framework — that consent is insufficient protection and accountability must rest with data *controllers*, not data *subjects* — becomes FF's preferred policy position on privacy. — SOURCE: "Consent isn't enough to protect data. We need accountability" by NS Ramnath (2017-08-10); "The future of privacy" by Founding Fuel (2017-09-17)

**Abilene Paradox:** Cited in the context of Murthy's echo chamber: "When you surround yourself with people who mirror your values and perspectives, you are inside an echo chamber." — SOURCE: "The unfolding Infosys leadership paradox" by K Ramkumar (2017-08-20)

**"Do not wrestle with pigs":** A recurring aphorism FF uses to explain why engaging with bad-faith actors is counterproductive. — SOURCE: "Two idiots and three pigs" by Charles Assisi (2017-05-05); "The myth that is the Indian liberal" by Charles Assisi (2017-06-03)

# Dense Observations: Founding Fuel on Philosophy & Ethics (Batch 3: 2017-12-03 to 2019-12-18)

---

## ARGUMENTS FF MAKES REPEATEDLY

**1. The purpose crisis in capitalism and business**

The single most repeated argument across this batch: business has lost its sense of purpose and is causing systemic harm. This manifests in multiple forms:

- Milton Friedman's "business of business is only business" is identified as the root pathology. "The dominant view was that the purpose of a business enterprise is to produce value for shareholders" — SOURCE: "The purpose of the enterprise" by Arun Maira (2018-02-01)
- "Leaders of large-scale projects [focus on] 'get it done'—whether in military campaigns or humanitarian relief projects; building large irrigation systems and dams or large communication systems; the conduct of elections or the rolling out of a universal biometric identification in a country with over a billion people. 'Execution is nine-tenths of strategy'" — SOURCE: "The purpose of the enterprise" by Arun Maira (2018-02-01)
